# FDG4014

> DO define a protected or an internal constructor in abstract classes.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 4.4 Abstract Class Design.

## How it is checked

- Check: sdk (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: CA1012
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: draft

CA1012 reports a public constructor on an externally visible abstract type. An abstract class with no declared constructor complies: the C# compiler gives it a protected one. Making the constructor protected changes the public API, so the fix is breaking.

## From the book

A protected constructor is more common and simply allows the base class to do its own initialization when subtypes are created.

```csharp
public abstract class Claim {
  protected Claim() {
    ...
  }
}
```

An internal constructor can be used to limit concrete implementations of the abstract class to the assembly defining the class.

```csharp
public abstract class Claim {
  internal Claim() {
    ...
  }
}
```

> **Brad Abrams:** Many languages (such as C#) will insert a protected constructor if you do not. It is a good practice to define the constructor explicitly in the source so that it can be more easily documented and maintained over time.
